items.q: Word Search II — trie-pruned grid search
shortAnswer: Return all words from a list that can be built from adjacent grid cells, each cell used at most once per word.
Build a trie of the words, then DFS the grid once, passing the trie node down and pruning the moment a child letter is absent.
The gotchas are dedup — clear each collected word — and in-place `#` marking for visited cells. The trie prunes hard, beating per-word DFS.
items.prompt:
Given a `board: Array<CharArray>` and a `List<String>` of words, return all words that can be built from adjacent (up/down/left/right) cells, each cell used at most once per word.

Naive: run the single-word DFS (Word Search I) for each word — O(words × board × 4^len). The trick is to build a trie of all words first and walk the grid once, pruning branches the moment the current prefix stops being a trie prefix. That's the difference between an interview answer that scales and one that doesn't.
hints: Running DFS per word is correct but slow. What structure can answer 'is this prefix worth pursuing?' in O(1)?
A trie of the word list. DFS over the grid, extending the current trie node as you move cells.
Pass the trie node down the recursion; if a child letter is absent, prune. Mark cells visited with a temp char to avoid per-path visited sets; collect full words when you reach an end-of-word node.

code.caption: Trie-pruned grid DFS

items.complexity: Time O(rows·cols·4·L) in practice — each grid cell starts a DFS that gets pruned by the trie; worst case is better than the per-word O(W·4^L). Space O(total word chars) for the trie plus recursion depth.
followUps: Why set `child.word = null` after collecting? (Duplicate words from different paths.)
What if words overlap heavily — how does the trie amortize the cost?
Backtracking with a visited set vs in-place '#' mutation — trade-offs?

shortAnswer: Deep-copy an undirected graph and return a copy of the starting node.
DFS with a `HashMap` from original node to copy, checked before recursing — the map breaks the cycle.
Without the map, undirected edges recurse forever on cycles. Time O(V + E), space O(V).
items.prompt:
Given a reference to a node in an undirected graph (each node has a value and a list of neighbors), deep-copy the entire graph and return a copy of the starting node.

Cycles make naive recursion loop forever — you need a visited map from original node to its copy. This is the canonical "graph deep copy" and the same map discipline as ds-0036 (copy list with random pointer).
hints: Copying the root then recursing on neighbors loops forever on cycles. What breaks the cycle?
A `HashMap<Node, Node>` from original to copy, checked before recursing: if we've made it, return the copy.
Use DFS or BFS; the map is the identity. First touch of a node: create its copy, put it in the map, then process neighbors through `map.getOrPut`.

code.caption: DFS with a visited map — O(V + E)

items.complexity: Time O(V + E), space O(V) for the map plus recursion depth. State that the map is the entire trick — without it, undirected edges recurse forever.
followUps: What happens without the visited map on a two-node cycle?
BFS version — where does the map check go?
Clone a *directed* graph — does anything change?
items.sampleCall:
run {
    val one = GNode(1); val two = GNode(2); val three = GNode(3); val four = GNode(4)
    one.neighbors.addAll(listOf(two, four)); two.neighbors.addAll(listOf(one, three))
    three.neighbors.addAll(listOf(two, four)); four.neighbors.addAll(listOf(one, three))
    val copy = cloneGraph(one)!!
    copy.value.toString() + " with " + copy.neighbors.size + " neighbors"
}

shortAnswer: Return the length of the shortest word transformation sequence, one letter per step, through words in a list.
This is unweighted shortest path, so BFS: at each position try every letter, look up neighbors in a set, and remove them as visited.
Generate neighbors cheaply — 26·L set lookups per word, not a scan of the list. Bidirectional BFS is the level-4 differentiator to name.
items.prompt:
Given `beginWord`, `endWord`, and a `wordList`, return the length of the shortest transformation sequence from `begin` to `end`, where each step changes exactly one letter and every intermediate word must be in the list. Return 0 if impossible.

The insight: this is unweighted shortest path on a graph of words — BFS. The optimization (bidirectional BFS) is the level-4 differentiator; mention it even if you code the one-directional version first.
hints: Model each word as a node, edges between words differing by one letter. Shortest path in an unweighted graph = BFS.
Enumerate neighbors cheaply: for each position, replace the letter with every 'a'..'z' and look up in a set — O(26·L) per word instead of O(words).
Level count: BFS in layers, distance + 1 per layer. Then say: bidirectional BFS from both ends cuts the frontier dramatically.

code.caption: BFS over wildcard neighbors — O(n·26·L)

items.complexity: Time O(n · 26 · L) for the one-directional BFS (n words, L length), space O(n). Bidirectional BFS is the same worst case but typically far fewer expansions — the expected interview follow-up.
followUps: Return the actual transformation path, not just the length.
Bidirectional BFS — when does it really win?
What if 'begin' is also in the list — does removal-as-visited break anything?

items.q: Network Delay Time — single-source shortest path
shortAnswer: Return the time until all nodes receive a signal from node `k` over weighted edges, or -1 if any is unreachable.
Run Dijkstra with a min-heap keyed by distance, relax edges, skip stale heap entries, and take the maximum settled distance.
The gotcha is that weighted edges rule out BFS, and 'all nodes' means max of shortest paths. O(E log V); explain the stale-entry skip.
items.prompt:
You have `n` nodes and `times: List<IntArray>` of `[u, v, w]` directed edges with transmission delays. Starting from node `k`, return the time it takes for *all* nodes to receive the signal, or -1 if any node is unreachable.

Classic Dijkstra. Two things to say out loud: the graph is weighted (so BFS is wrong), and "time for all nodes" is the maximum of the shortest paths — i.e. run Dijkstra and take the max distance.
hints: Weights are non-negative and we need shortest paths from one source to all nodes — which algorithm?
Dijkstra with a min-heap keyed by distance. Relax edges: if `dist[u] + w < dist[v]`, update and push.
Answer = max over all `dist[]` values that got set; if any node still has infinity, return -1.

code.caption: Dijkstra with a min-heap — O(E log V)

items.complexity: Time O(E log V), space O(V + E). Mention the stale-entry skip (`if d > dist[u] continue`) — interviewers love to see it explained rather than written by rote.
followUps: Why can't BFS handle weighted edges?
What if some edges have negative weights? (Dijkstra breaks — Bellman-Ford.)
Return the path from k to a target node, not just the time.

items.q: Course Schedule II — return a valid order
shortAnswer: Return a valid order to take all courses given prerequisites, or an empty list if a cycle makes it impossible.
Kahn's algorithm: enqueue zero in-degree courses, pop one into the result, decrement neighbors, and enqueue any reaching zero.
The cycle check is automatic — fewer than `numCourses` processed means impossibility. Time O(V + E), space O(V + E).
items.prompt:
There are `n` courses labeled 0..n-1 and prerequisites `[[a,b]]` meaning course `b` must be taken before `a`. Return a valid ordering of all courses, or an empty list if it's impossible.

Course Schedule I (ds-0011) just asks *can* you finish; this one asks for the actual topological order. Kahn's algorithm (in-degree + queue) or DFS with colors. You should be able to write Kahn's and explain cycle detection in the same breath.
hints: Topological order = an ordering where every edge points forward. When the graph is a DAG, Kahn's works.
Compute in-degrees, enqueue all in-degree-0 nodes. Pop one, append to result, decrement its neighbors' in-degrees, enqueue any that hit 0.
If the result has fewer than n nodes, there was a cycle — return an empty list. That's the impossibility check.

code.caption: Kahn's algorithm — O(V + E)

items.complexity: Time O(V + E), space O(V + E) for adjacency plus O(V) for the queue and result. Kahn's is the answer to prefer on the board — it makes the cycle check automatic.
followUps: How does the result size detect a cycle? Trace a 2-node cycle.
Return the lexicographically smallest valid order (use a min-heap instead of a queue).
DFS-with-colors variant — where does a back edge signal the cycle?

items.q: Redundant Connection — find the edge that closes a cycle
shortAnswer: Find the edge whose removal restores a tree, from a graph with exactly one extra edge.
Union-find with path compression: add edges one at a time, and the first edge whose endpoints are already connected is the answer.
The input-order guarantee is the whole trick — the first cycle-closing edge is the last removable one in the input. Near O(n) with `α(n)`.
items.prompt:
A tree of `n` nodes has exactly one extra edge added, producing a graph with exactly one cycle. Given the edge list `edges: Array<IntArray>` in order, return the edge that appears last in the input and could be removed to restore a tree.

Union-Find with path compression is the intended answer: add edges one at a time; the first edge whose two endpoints are *already connected* is the answer. Learn this alongside ds-0012 (number of islands) — they share the same data structure.
hints: Adding edges one by one, a cycle forms the moment you connect two nodes already in the same set.
Union-Find: `find(x)` with path compression, `union(a, b)`. Iterate edges; if `find(a) == find(b)`, that edge is redundant.
Use a `parent: IntArray` initialized to `it`, and union by rank or size to keep the tree shallow.

code.caption: Union-Find with path compression — near O(n)

items.complexity: Time O(n · α(n)) with path compression (inverse-Ackermann, effectively constant), space O(n). The DFS-with-visit-set alternative is O(n²) because it re-traverses per edge.
followUps: Why 'last edge in input order' — what does the ordering guarantee?
Return the edge that would break the graph into two components instead (same set check).
Path compression alone vs union by rank — what does each buy?

shortAnswer: Place `n` queens on an n×n board so none attack, and return all distinct solutions as boards.
Place one queen per row, checking column, `r - c`, and `r + c` in O(1), pruning the moment a placement is illegal.
The O(1) attack checks — two diagonal formulas instead of board scans — plus backtracking by unmarking. Worst case O(n!) with pruning.
items.prompt:
Place `n` queens on an n×n board so no two attack each other (same row, column, or diagonal). Return all distinct solutions as boards of '.' and 'Q'.

The canonical constraint-backtracking problem. The level-4 crux is tracking the three attack lines (column, main diagonal, anti-diagonal) with arrays so the check is O(1), and pruning as soon as a placement is illegal — never filling a full board to test it.
hints: Place one queen per row, and only try safe columns. This already prevents same-row and same-column attacks.
A queen attacks along diagonals too. Two cells `(r,c)` and `(r2,c2)` share a diagonal iff `r-c` (main) or `r+c` (anti) are equal — track both with sets.
Recursion: at row r, try each safe column, mark the three lines, recurse, then unmark (backtrack). Collect when r == n.

code.caption: Backtracking with attack-line sets — O(n!)

items.complexity: Time O(n!) worst case (n queens, pruning helps), space O(n) for the recursion plus the output. The O(1) attack checks — three lines instead of scanning the board — are the point of the exercise.
followUps: Why `r-c` and `r+c` for the diagonals? Convince with an example.
Return the count of solutions only (N-Queens II) — same engine.
How does the pruning change if queens are all in the same row to start (n-rooks)?
